say.text: Radioiodine treats remnant and iodine-avid metastatic differentiated cancer.
Before the dose, what must drive those cells to take up iodine?

choices.label: TSH, released by the pituitary, drives uptake
Iodine dose alone; no hormone drives uptake
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Think about the signal the brain sends the thyroid to make it work harder. Which signal is that?
Yes. Uptake needs a high TSH level, above 30 mU/L, so a raised TSH is the state radioiodine needs.
Every later step in this ladder builds on that one state.
That choice is not right. It tempts because suppressed TSH is the goal after surgery, so it feels like the normal state of a treated patient.
But a suppressed signal is the wrong state for uptake, as the uptake claim shows. Check the level the dose needs.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so fix the state the dose needs: suppression is the after-surgery goal, not the pre-dose state.

say.text: That choice is not right. It tempts because iodine is what the dose delivers, so the dose feels like the only variable that matters.
But the dose alone does not set uptake. Uptake depends on a raised level of a hormone signal, so the dose is given only after that level is reached.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so this is the belief to fix: uptake is a signal problem before it is an iodine-dose problem.

say.text: So TSH must be high on the day of the dose, and two routes can get it there.
Which step raises TSH before the dose?

choices.label: Stop levothyroxine for weeks, or give recombinant TSH
Raise levothyroxine so TSH is pushed lower first
Add an extra thyroxine tablet on the day of dose
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: The pituitary answers to the thyroid hormone in the blood. Which way would that blood level have to move for the pituitary to shout?
Yes. Withdrawing levothyroxine for a few weeks, or giving recombinant human TSH, lifts TSH above 30 mU/L for uptake.
A low-iodine diet is added beforehand to help the uptake.
That choice is not right. It tempts because tighter suppression sounds like better preparation for treating cancer cells.
But uptake needs a raised TSH, so pushing TSH lower works against the dose. The direction of the change is wrong.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so fix the direction: the pre-dose step moves TSH up, not down.

say.text: That choice is not right. It tempts because an extra tablet looks like a quick way to change the level on the day.
But extra thyroxine lowers TSH, and a lower TSH gives weaker uptake. The step has to raise the level, as the uptake claim shows.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check the direction of the TSH change before the dose, not the drug name.

say.text: A patient has had total thyroidectomy for papillary cancer and starts levothyroxine.
What is its main job for the cancer?

choices.label: Suppress TSH, because TSH stimulates residual cancer growth
Lower TSH before the dose, so the cells take up more
Replace the hormone only; TSH level does not matter
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Ask what the tablet does to the pituitary signal once the thyroid is gone, and why that signal matters for a cancer.
Yes. Levothyroxine replaces the hormone and holds TSH down, because TSH stimulates residual DTC growth.
That choice is not right. It tempts because the same drug holds TSH down, so a pre-dose step looks like more of the same.
But suppression is the job after surgery. Before the dose, uptake needs TSH to rise, so lowering it first blunts the treatment.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so keep the two phases apart: pre-dose and post-surgery goals are opposite on TSH.

say.text: That choice is not right. It tempts because replacing the hormone is the visible job of the tablet, so the TSH number feels like a side issue.
But TSH is the lever the drug controls, and TSH stimulates cancer growth. That is why the level is watched.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check whether TSH has a role in the cancer, not only in the thyroid.

say.text: Patient A has low-risk unifocal disease, 1.5 cm, with no nodes or extension.
Patient B has gross extension through the thyroid capsule. Which TSH target fits each?

choices.label: A low-normal TSH; B below 0.1 mU/L
Below 0.1 mU/L for both, to be safe
Low-normal for both, since over-suppression harms
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Work out each patient's ATA risk class first. Then ask how far TSH needs to fall for that class.
Yes. Risk sets the target. Low-risk disease needs low-normal TSH, while high-risk disease needs deeper suppression, below 0.1 mU/L.
That choice is not right. It tempts because deeper suppression sounds safer, so one firm target feels easier to remember.
But low-risk disease does not need the deeper suppression. The target is matched to the ATA class, not set once for everyone.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so this is one target for everyone; check which class each patient is in first.

say.text: That choice is not right. It tempts because over-treatment with thyroxine feels harmful, so the lowest safe level looks like the one target.
But patient B is high risk, and that class is driven to a lower TSH than low-risk disease. One target for both misses that.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check whether the target follows the disease class or a general rule of caution.

say.text: A 45-year-old has a 2 cm papillary cancer, unifocal and intrathyroidal, with no nodes or distant spread. Total thyroidectomy is done.
Is radioiodine given routinely?

choices.label: Not routinely; low-risk disease does not need it
Yes, as standard adjuvant for every DTC patient
Only if the tumour is follicular, not papillary
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Ask which ATA class this patient falls into, and what that class says about radioiodine.
Yes. Radioiodine follows the ATA risk class, and a low-risk patient is not routinely given it.
That choice is not right. It tempts because radioiodine is the familiar follow-on after thyroid cancer surgery, so it feels like a default.
But the default is the risk class. For ATA low-risk disease, radioiodine is not routinely used.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check the risk class before you reach for a routine adjuvant.

say.text: That choice is not right. It tempts because papillary and follicular are taught side by side, so the histology feels like the switch.
But histology does not decide it. The risk class, which covers size, spread and extension, does.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so the cancer type is not the trigger; the risk class is.

say.text: Patient A: 1.2 cm unifocal papillary cancer, no nodes, no extension. Patient B: 4 cm with gross extension through the capsule.
Which pair of plans fits?

choices.label: A: lobectomy or total. B: total, then ablation
Both: total thyroidectomy, the classic answer for DTC surgery
A: total, then ablation as standard. B: total, then ablation
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Sort each patient by size, spread and extension first. Then ask what each class needs for surgery and for radioiodine.
Yes. Size and extent set the operation: low-risk tumours of 1–4 cm may have lobectomy, while gross extension needs total thyroidectomy.
Radioiodine follows the class too: none routinely for patient A, and ablation for patient B.
That choice is not right. It tempts because total thyroidectomy was the expected answer in older papers, so one operation feels safe for both.
But the operation follows size and extent, and ATA 2015 accepts lobectomy for low-risk tumours of 1–4 cm.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so this is the old key talking: PYQs expected total thyroidectomy, while current practice sizes the operation.

say.text: That choice is not right. It tempts because ablation is the familiar step after total thyroidectomy, so it feels like part of the package.
But ablation follows risk, not the operation. Patient A is low risk, and low-risk disease is not routinely given radioiodine.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so separate the two decisions: the operation and the radioiodine each follow their own rule.

say.text: The ladder: radioiodine needs a raised TSH before the dose, and levothyroxine holds TSH low afterwards.
The TSH target and the radioiodine decision both follow the ATA risk class, not one rule for every patient.
Two phases have opposite goals. After surgery, TSH is held low. Before the radioiodine dose, TSH must be high.
Uptake by thyroid cells follows TSH. A suppressed TSH gives poor uptake, so the dose needs a raised level.
Think of the pituitary as a thermostat. A high thyroxine level tells it to cut TSH, and a low level makes it release more.
So the pre-dose step must lower thyroxine, by withdrawing levothyroxine, or add recombinant TSH.
Levothyroxine given after surgery holds TSH down, because TSH can drive any residual cancer cells.
The pre-dose goal is the reverse: TSH is raised. Keep the two phases apart.
The TSH target is matched to the ATA risk class. Low-risk disease is held at low-normal TSH.
Only high-risk disease, such as gross extension, needs deeper suppression below 0.1 mU/L. One target for all is the error.
Radioiodine follows the risk class, not the diagnosis alone. Low-risk disease is not routinely given it.
Here the tumour is 2 cm, unifocal, intrathyroidal and node-negative, so it is low risk and ablation is not routine.
Two separate decisions apply. The operation follows size and extent. Radioiodine follows risk class.
Patient A, low risk at 1.2 cm, may have lobectomy and no routine ablation. Patient B, with gross extension, needs total thyroidectomy then ablation.
